text: Stand near a wall or a worktop, close enough to touch it. Stand on one foot and count. Now try it with your eyes closed. Most people last a fraction as long — that is how much of your balance was coming from your eyes without you knowing.

text: Hold your arm out and touch your nose with your eyes shut. You didn't look and you didn't miss. That's a whole sense most people never notice they have.

text: Rub your hands together fast for ten seconds. That warmth is friction becoming heat — the same reason moving on a cold day works better than another jumper.

review.notes: Safe, performable, and it teaches a real thing (heart rate is demand-driven). Wrist pulse rather than carotid, mild activity, no dose or comparative claim to overreach on.

text: Find your pulse at your wrist, count for fifteen seconds, multiply by four. Now stand up, do twenty marches, and count again. You just watched your heart respond to a demand.

review.notes: Two problems. The instruction is ambiguous - 'press your finger' does not say press what against what (the nail bed, held a couple of seconds). And 'it takes about a second' is a dose stated more precisely than the evidence: published medians are ~0.8s for young men but ~1.5-1.8s for elderly readers, and cold ambient temperature roughly doubles it (median 1.3s warm vs 2.9s after cold immersion). A senior or a reader with cold hands will get 3 seconds and conclude something is wrong with them.

text: Press your finger and watch the color come back. That's your blood refilling capillaries you just squeezed empty, and it takes about a second.

review.notes: The safety hedge is good, but the experiment cannot show what it claims. A second toe-reach goes further than the first from stretch tolerance and the repeated-bout effect alone, with no warming involved, so the demo attributes to temperature a change that would happen anyway. 'One walk is enough to feel it' also fixes a dose (two minutes) that nobody has measured for this; warm-up ROM studies generally use far longer.

text: Reach down toward your toes — only as far as is comfortable, and stop well before anything pulls. Note where you got to, walk for two minutes, and try again. Warm muscle reaches further than cold muscle, and one walk is enough to feel it.

review.notes: True mechanics (widening the base of support improves lateral stability), safe, and the stepladder analogy genuinely explains rather than restates. No unearned comparative - 'steadier' is the whole point and is correct.

text: Stand with your feet together, then a shoulder-width apart. The second one feels obviously steadier. That's your base of support, and it's the same reason a stepladder's legs splay out.

review.notes: The arm-swing mechanism is real, but two defects. 'It feels obviously wrong' is asserted as a universal subjective result that many readers will not get. More importantly, folding the arms while walking removes the arm reactions an unsteady reader would use to catch themselves; 'a clear bit of floor' covers tripping but not that, and the audience includes seventy-year-olds. The text should name the risk or restrict the invitation.

text: Walk across a clear bit of floor. Now do it again with your arms folded. It feels wrong because your arms were doing work you never asked them to do.

review.notes: 'Notice you can't do it convincingly' is false for a large share of readers - voluntary yawns are common and frequently tip into genuine ones - so the item tells the reader their own result is wrong. The second half is not performable on demand (it requires somebody else to yawn while you watch). Calling contagious yawning a 'reflex' also states a mechanism that is still argued over, in an item labelled simplified rather than contested.

text: Yawn on purpose and notice you can't do it convincingly. Then watch somebody else yawn. One of those is a reflex and one is acting.

text: Look at something far away for twenty seconds after reading this. Your focusing muscle has been holding one position — that's most of why screens make eyes tired.

review.notes: Accurate and safe: the masseter is palpable exactly where the text says, clenching briefly carries no meaningful risk, and 'the muscle that bites' is a fair simplification at min_age 9. It teaches something a reader can verify on themselves in five seconds.

text: Clench your jaw and put your fingers just in front of your ears. That movement under your fingertips is the muscle that bites — and it is doing it every time you eat without you ever noticing.

review.notes: Safety: 'hopping if you like' is offered casually to an audience that includes seventy-year-olds, and no risk is named - single-leg hopping is a real fall and fracture risk for an older reader, and the hold-on/chair alternatives are framed as preferences rather than as the safe default. Separately, 'dozens of them' is an invented count for postural corrections nobody has measured in this context.

text: Shift your weight onto one foot — hopping if you like, near something to hold if you would rather, or just leaning in a chair. Feel the ankle making corrections you never decided to make, dozens of them, none of which reached your attention.

text: Breathe out slowly for twice as long as you breathe in, three times. Your heart rate drops slightly on every exhale, which is the whole trick behind slow breathing.

review.notes: The payload claim is unsupported folklore in plausible dress. 'The drop afterwards is lower than where you started' is a measurable postural outcome nobody has measured, and the general law 'muscles relax further after being asked to tighten' comes from post-isometric relaxation, where the documented effect is a transient depression of spinal reflex excitability that has recovered by about five seconds - not a lasting drop in resting shoulder position. The whole item is that claim, stated as certain fact.

text: Shrug your shoulders as high as they go, hold for five seconds, then let go. The drop afterwards is lower than where you started — muscles relax further after being asked to tighten.

review.notes: Two firmness problems. 'You are measurably taller now than you'll be tonight' assumes the reader is opening the app in the morning; over 50% of daily height loss occurs within the first hour of rising and 80% within three hours, so the statement is simply false for an afternoon reader. And 'about a centimetre' understates the usual figure - total diurnal stature loss is around 1.5-2 cm, or roughly 1% of height.

text: Stand up and reach for the ceiling. You are measurably taller now than you'll be tonight: the discs in your spine compress about a centimetre over a day and plump back up while you sleep.
